Indignation

/in-dig-NAY-shuhn/ - the stress falls on NAY · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Indignation means anger sparked by something unjust or unfair.

Fans erupted in indignation when the ticket site's mandatory 'convenience' fees turned out to double the listed price.

Worked Example

One student glued the trophy case shut; the principal canceled the spring trip for all four hundred. By evening the indignation had its own group chat: honor students who had never met were drafting petitions, and parents who disagreed about everything else agreed, loudly, that four hundred should not pay for one.

Indignation is the exact word because it names anger sparked by unfairness — anger that argues. The students aren't just deprived and sulking; they have a rule of fairness in hand, and the collective punishment offends it. When anger can point at the injustice that lit it, indignation is its name.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

outrage: indignation turned up loud — hotter and more public

resentment: quiet and nursed in private; indignation flares and speaks up

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

approval: the judgment that things were done fairly

delight: open pleasure at how things went

Where it sits · how loudly the sense of wrong speaks — displeasure → indignation → outrage

displeasure vs. indignation: Displeasure notes that it isn't pleased and leaves it there; indignation has found the unfairness and means to say so.

outrage vs. indignation: Outrage goes past indignation — the anger has filled the square and stopped counting its words.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — in-

Prefix — in-: not

Root — dign

Root — dign: worthy (Latin dignus)

Suffix — -ation

Suffix — -ation: state of

Put it together

Put it together: In- (not) + dign (worthy — Latin dignus) + -ation (state of) = the state of being treated as not worthy. Indignation is the noun for the whole event: worth denied, wrong perceived, anger answering. English has kept the pair together for six centuries — the indignant feel indignation.

Use the root in a new word: dignitary

Use the root in a new word: dignitary: A dignitary is literally a person of worth — the same root wearing a sash.

Word Choice

neutral / formal

Indignation is the noun for anger with an injustice at the bottom of it; the adjective is this unit's indignant. It flares and goes public — petitions, letters, speeches. When the anger stays private and slow-burning, the truer word is resentment, and when it boils past argument into the streets, outrage has taken over.
